lesson.title: A Young Frenchman's Cause: The Marquis de Lafayette
lesson.summary: The French aristocrat Marquis de Lafayette crossed the Atlantic to fight for American independence, became one of George Washington's most trusted officers, and helped secure the French support that made victory at Yorktown possible.
lesson.body:
Gilbert du Motier, the Marquis de Lafayette, was born in 1757 into a wealthy French noble family and inherited both a title and a considerable fortune while still a child, having lost his father in battle when he was young. Drawn to the American cause partly by genuine belief in its ideals of liberty and partly by a desire for military glory, Lafayette defied French royal orders restricting travel to America and sailed for the colonies, arriving in 1777 at his own expense aboard a ship he had purchased himself. He was still only nineteen years old at the time.

Impressed by his enthusiasm and his family's standing, and eager to encourage further French support for the Revolution, the Second Continental Congress commissioned Lafayette as a major general, initially an honorary rank given his youth and inexperience. He soon won a genuine field command, however, and quickly built a close personal relationship with George Washington, who came to regard the young Frenchman almost as a son and who had no children of his own. Lafayette was wounded in the leg at the Battle of Brandywine in September 1777 while helping organize an orderly retreat, an early sign of the courage that would define his American service.

Lafayette shared in the hardships of the army's difficult winter at Valley Forge in 1777 and 1778, living alongside the troops rather than seeking more comfortable quarters elsewhere, which helped cement his reputation among American soldiers as a committed and sincere ally rather than a visiting dignitary passing through. His presence, and his connections back home, also helped strengthen the case for direct French intervention, which arrived formally with the Franco American alliance of February 1778, a turning point that followed the American victory at Saratoga the previous autumn.

In 1779 Lafayette returned briefly to France to lobby the French court for greater military support, and he came back to America in 1780 with news of additional French troops and, eventually, naval forces under experienced commanders. His efforts helped bring about the combined Franco American operation that trapped British General Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, in the fall of 1781. Lafayette commanded American forces in Virginia in the campaign leading up to the siege, working alongside the French army under the Comte de Rochambeau and the French fleet under the Comte de Grasse to seal Cornwallis's fate, which ended in his surrender on October 19, 1781.

Lafayette returned to France a hero of the American cause and remained a lifelong symbol of the alliance between the two nations, later playing a prominent, though more turbulent, role in the early years of the French Revolution. His story illustrates how the ideals articulated in the Declaration of Independence resonated well beyond America's own borders, inspiring foreign volunteers to risk their lives and fortunes for a cause not originally their own.
